newsitem.title: USA: Credibility is new focus of U.S. abortion war.
newsitem.headline: Credibility is new focus of U.S. abortion war.

text.p: The U.S. political war over so-called partial birth abortion has a new battleground: the ebbing credibility of advocates who now say the procedure is neither rare nor confined to women and foetuses at risk.

Even as a new measure to ban the controversial medical procedure was introduced on Wednesday in the House of Representatives, abortion rights advocates worked to dispel what they called a "misimpression" about the issue.

"A pro-choice lobbyist's announcement that he lied about the number of so-called partial birth abortions has further confused the facts regarding legislation to ban the abortion procedure," Kate Michelman, president of the National Abortion and Reproductive Rights Action League, said in a statement.

"... In responding to the erroneous claims made by supporters of the abortion ban, we may have given rise to the misimpression that the procedure was only done in the third trimester. That was not our intention," Michelman said.

The issue has sparked heated debate since a ban was first introduced in Congress in 1995, possibly because of the nature of the procedure, which involves the partial extraction of the foetus, feet-first, from the birth canal and the subsequent suctioning out of the foetal brain and removal of the foetus.

The latest flareup began last week when Ron Fitzsimmons, executive director of the National Coalition of Abortion Providers, said he "lied through my teeth" when he defended this kind of late-term abortion.

In an article published on Tuesday in American Medical News, Fitzsimmons said most of these abortions -- referred to medically as intact dilation and evacuation -- were performed on healthy women with healthy foetuses.

"The pro-choice movement has lost a lot of credibility during this debate, not just with the general public, but with our pro-choice friends in Congress," Fitzsimmons told the News, a publication of the American Medical Association. "Even the White House is now questioning the accuracy of some of the information given to it on this issue."

President Bill Clinton vetoed a proposed ban on the procedure last April, arguing that it was performed on only a few hundred women whose health was endangered or whose foetuses had terrible deformities. To drive home his point, he vetoed the measure surrounded by women who had had the procedure and had wrenching testimony about why it was required.

Clinton said he would sign the bill if it included an exception for cases where the woman's health was at risk. The current bill, like the previous one, provides only for cases where the woman's life, but not her health, is in jeopardy.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry on Wednesday said Clinton was willing to work with Congress to craft a measure he could sign.

But Representative Nita Lowey, a New York Democrat, said Republicans were unwilling to compromise. "We know from experience that the Republicans don't want a law -- they want a political issue," Lowey said in a statement.

What has never been clear is the actual number of these procedures performed in the United States. The National Abortion Federation has estimated it at less than 500 annually but Representative Charles Canady, a Florida Republican who introduced the new bill in the House, said there may be thousands.
